difficultyReason: Requires identifying the principle that licenses a normative claim about medical disclosure; distractors invoke plausible but tangential duties.
stimulus: Physician: A patient asked me whether a new cholesterol medication I was prescribing carries any risk of liver damage. I told her it does not, even though recent trial data suggest a small but nonzero risk. My reason was that disclosing a very small risk would cause the patient needless anxiety and would likely lead her to refuse a treatment she genuinely needs. This was the right decision.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the physician's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A physician is obligated to tell patients only information that the physician has verified through direct clinical experience.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients should always be given the opportunity to seek a second opinion before beginning any new course of treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Withholding information from a patient is justified when disclosing it would cause harm that outweighs the benefit of the patient's being informed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physician who deceives a patient for any reason violates the fundamental duty of medical practice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Medical decisions should be guided primarily by the financial interests of the healthcare system rather than by the preferences of individual patients.

explanations.correct: The physician's argument rests on a harm-benefit calculation: the harm of the patient's anxiety and treatment refusal outweighs the benefit of knowing a tiny risk. Principle C captures this balancing logic directly and licenses the conclusion that withholding was right.
explanations.A: Tangential — the issue is not verification of information but whether to disclose it. This principle addresses a different condition entirely.
explanations.B: Tangential — second opinions are not mentioned or implied by the physician's reasoning.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle would condemn the physician's action, not justify it.
explanations.E: Too broad and mismatched — financial interests of the healthcare system play no role in the physician's stated reasoning.

difficultyReason: Argument turns on a specific normative move about regulatory burden; distractors are plausibly related to environmental policy but miss the argument's core.
stimulus: Environmentalist: The proposed coastal development project would destroy approximately forty hectares of protected wetlands. Developers argue that the economic benefits to the region justify proceeding. But the project should not be approved. The economic gains will accrue primarily to a small group of private investors, while the ecological losses — erosion protection, flood mitigation, and biodiversity — will be borne by the entire coastal community for generations.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the environmentalist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Economic development should never be permitted in areas designated as protected habitat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A project that concentrates benefits among a few private parties while distributing its costs broadly across the public is not justified on economic grounds alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ecological value of wetlands is always greater than any economic benefit a development project could produce.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Private investors who profit from development projects should be required to compensate local communities for any resulting inconvenience.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory agencies are obligated to solicit public comment before approving any coastal construction project.

explanations.correct: The environmentalist's argument hinges on an asymmetry: private parties capture the benefits while the public bears the costs. Principle B — that such asymmetric distribution defeats an economic justification — licenses the conclusion that approval is unwarranted.
explanations.A: Too broad — the environmentalist does not claim all development in protected areas is impermissible; the objection is specifically about who bears costs versus who gains benefits.
explanations.C: Too broad — the environmentalist does not argue that ecological value universally trumps economic benefit; the argument is specifically about the distribution of gains and losses.
explanations.D: Tangential — compensation mechanisms are not what the environmentalist invokes; the argument opposes approval, not inadequate compensation.
explanations.E: Tangential — procedural public-comment requirements are unrelated to the substantive cost-benefit reasoning offered.

difficultyReason: The normative claim involves authenticity and artistic intent; distractors exploit adjacent aesthetic concepts without licensing the specific conclusion.
stimulus: Critic: The symphony orchestra's decision to use computer-generated sound effects during a live performance of a contemporary orchestral work is artistically indefensible. The composer explicitly scored the piece for acoustic instruments only, and the audience paid to hear a live acoustic performance. Substituting synthesized sounds — even imperceptible ones — misrepresents what the audience is experiencing.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the critic's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contemporary composers should always collaborate with performers to determine the final sonic character of a new work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An arts organization acts wrongly when it presents a performance in a manner that misrepresents the nature of what the audience will experience.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Computer-generated music is inherently inferior in artistic quality to music performed by live acoustic instruments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ticket prices for orchestral performances should reflect the full costs of production, including any technology used.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A composer's intentions are relevant to a performance's artistic merit only when those intentions are communicated to the audience in advance.

explanations.correct: The critic's argument centers on misrepresentation: the audience believes they are hearing an acoustic performance but are not. Principle B — that presenting a performance in a way that misrepresents what the audience experiences is wrong — directly licenses the conclusion that the orchestra's decision is indefensible.
explanations.A: Tangential — composer-performer collaboration during composition is not what the critic invokes; the issue is what occurs during a live performance.
explanations.C: Too broad — the critic does not claim synthesized sound is inherently inferior; the objection is about misrepresentation, not the quality of the technology.
explanations.D: Tangential — ticket pricing and cost transparency are unrelated to the critic's misrepresentation argument.
explanations.E: Reversed — this principle would weaken the critic's position by implying the composer's intent is irrelevant unless disclosed to the audience.

difficultyReason: The argument involves a normative claim about legal accountability; distractors invoke related legal concepts but fail to match the argument's logical structure.
stimulus: Legal Scholar: A software company released a security update that it knew contained an unpatched vulnerability, reasoning that the vulnerability was unlikely to be exploited before a full fix was ready. When the vulnerability was exploited two weeks later and users' financial data was stolen, the company claimed it bore no legal responsibility because it had acted in good faith. This claim is wrong. The company was aware of the risk it was imposing on its users and chose to impose it anyway.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the legal scholar's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Software companies should be held to a higher standard of care than other technology firms because of the sensitive nature of financial data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Good faith is a complete defense to legal liability whenever a party lacked the intent to cause harm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A party that knowingly imposes a risk of harm on others bears legal responsibility if that risk materializes, regardless of the party's intentions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Companies operating in the technology sector are responsible for ensuring that all software they release is completely free of security vulnerabilities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal liability arises only when a party's conduct falls below the standard that a reasonable person would observe in the same situation.

explanations.correct: The scholar's argument is that knowing about a risk and choosing to impose it defeats the good-faith defense — awareness of risk, not intent to harm, is what matters. Principle C captures this precisely: knowingly imposing a risk that materializes grounds liability regardless of intentions.
explanations.A: Too narrow — heightened standards for financial-data companies are not the scholar's basis for rejecting the good-faith defense; the argument applies to knowing risk-imposition generally.
explanations.B: Reversed — this principle would support the company's claim, which is exactly what the scholar is arguing against.
explanations.D: Too broad — requiring zero vulnerabilities is far stronger than the scholar's claim, which is only about knowing about a risk; the scholar does not require perfection.
explanations.E: Tangential — the reasonable-person standard may be relevant in negligence law, but the scholar's argument is specifically about the legal effect of the company's actual knowledge of the risk.

difficultyReason: Argument involves a normative claim about economic policy and individual circumstance; one distractor is temptingly close but addresses a different normative dimension.
stimulus: Economist: The proposed flat consumption tax would impose the same percentage rate on all purchases regardless of the buyer's income level. Proponents argue that equal percentage rates constitute equal treatment. But the policy is unfair. A family spending ninety percent of its income on necessities loses a far greater share of its discretionary resources to such a tax than does a household spending thirty percent of its income on those same goods.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tax policy is fair only when it raises sufficient revenue to fund essential government services for all citizens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Equal numerical treatment does not constitute equal treatment when the practical burden it imposes differs substantially across individuals due to differences in their circumstances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Governments should never impose any form of taxation on goods that qualify as basic necessities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tax policy is fair if and only if wealthier individuals pay a higher total dollar amount in taxes than do lower-income individuals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Economic policies should be evaluated primarily by whether they promote overall growth in gross domestic product.

explanations.correct: The economist's argument is that identical percentage rates are not genuinely equal because the actual burden differs based on income and spending patterns. Principle B — that equal numerical treatment can fail to constitute genuine equality when circumstances differ — licenses that critique directly.
explanations.A: Tangential — revenue sufficiency is not the economist's concern; the argument is about the distributive fairness of the rate structure.
explanations.C: Too broad — the economist does not argue against all taxation of necessities; the argument is about the flat rate's unequal effective burden, not the taxability of necessities per se.
explanations.D: Too narrow and mismatched — the principle concerns total dollar amounts rather than the proportional burden on discretionary resources, which is the economist's actual focus.
explanations.E: Tangential — GDP growth is unrelated to the fairness argument the economist advances.

difficultyReason: Requires identifying the principle behind a normative claim about linguistic preservation policy; distractors address related cultural or political concerns without licensing the specific argument.
stimulus: Linguist: Several regional governments have adopted policies that fund instruction exclusively in the dominant national language, eliminating support for minority language education. Officials justify this by arguing that fluency in the national language improves employment prospects. But these policies are misguided. A community's language is inseparable from its cultural identity and oral traditions; extinguishing the language extinguishes the community itself.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Government education policy should be designed to maximize the average employment income of graduates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Policies that produce measurable economic benefits are justified even if they involve some cultural costs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A policy that eliminates something constitutive of a community's identity is not justified solely by the economic benefits it may produce.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minority communities are entitled to representation in any government body that makes decisions affecting their linguistic rights.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Governments should promote bilingualism rather than monolingualism as the standard for national educational systems.

explanations.correct: The linguist argues that the economic justification is insufficient because eliminating minority language education destroys something constitutive of the community's identity. Principle C — that a policy eliminating something constitutive of community identity cannot be justified by economic benefits alone — licenses that conclusion directly.
explanations.A: Reversed — this principle supports the officials' justification rather than the linguist's critique.
explanations.B: Reversed — this principle would undermine the linguist's argument by allowing economic benefits to override cultural costs.
explanations.D: Tangential — procedural representation rights are not part of the linguist's substantive argument about the policy's justification.
explanations.E: Too narrow — advocating bilingualism is a specific policy recommendation that goes beyond what the linguist's argument requires; the linguist's point is about the insufficiency of an economic rationale, not about a preferred policy alternative.

difficultyReason: Argument involves a historical judgment about moral responsibility; distractors invoke temporal or institutional distinctions that are plausible but don't license the specific claim.
stimulus: Historian: Some have argued that leaders of the colonial administration in question cannot be judged by contemporary moral standards because they acted in accordance with the norms of their era. But this reasoning fails. Those leaders had access to dissenting voices within their own society — abolitionists, indigenous advocates, and dissident clergy — who articulated precisely why the policies were wrong. Choosing to ignore those voices does not excuse the moral failure.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historical figures should be evaluated only by the standards that were dominant in their own societies, not by standards developed afterward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who deliberately disregards a moral critique that was available to them at the time of their actions cannot claim ignorance as a defense against moral judgment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The existence of dissent within a society is sufficient evidence that the majority view at the time was morally wrong.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Colonial administrators should be held to the same legal standards as elected government officials in democratic states.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Moral progress requires that later generations recognize and correct the errors of their predecessors.

explanations.correct: The historian's argument turns on the fact that the leaders had access to moral criticism and chose to ignore it, making the 'different era' defense inapplicable. Principle B — that deliberately disregarding available moral critique forfeits the ignorance defense — licenses this conclusion precisely.
explanations.A: Reversed — this principle supports the position the historian is arguing against.
explanations.C: Too broad — the historian does not claim the existence of dissent proves the majority was wrong; the point is narrower: that the leaders personally had access to the critique and ignored it.
explanations.D: Tangential — legal standards for colonial administrators versus elected officials are not what the historian invokes; the argument is about moral judgment.
explanations.E: Tangential — the duty of later generations to correct past errors is a different normative claim than the one licensing the historian's specific argument about individual moral responsibility.

difficultyReason: Normative claim about technology and privacy requires the right scope of principle; one distractor is temptingly close but applies to a broader class of cases than the argument requires.
stimulus: Ethicist: A major social media platform recently began using its users' private messages to train its artificial intelligence models, relying on a clause buried in its terms of service that users had agreed to when signing up. The platform argues it acted within its legal rights. Nonetheless, the practice is ethically wrong. Users who agreed to those terms had no reasonable expectation that their private conversations would be used in this way.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Technology companies should be prohibited by law from training artificial intelligence systems on any user-generated content.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consent obtained through terms of service is legally valid and therefore sufficient to render any subsequent use of user data ethically permissible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acting within one's legal rights is sufficient to establish that one's conduct is ethically acceptable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Using information in a way that reasonable people who provided it would not have anticipated is ethically impermissible, regardless of legal authorization.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ethical permissibility of data use depends on whether the data was collected from users in a domain that is inherently public rather than private.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is that legal authorization does not settle the ethical question when users' reasonable expectations were violated. Principle D — that using information in ways users could not reasonably have anticipated is ethically impermissible regardless of legal authorization — licenses the conclusion that the platform acted wrongly.
explanations.A: Too broad — an absolute prohibition on AI training from user content goes far beyond the ethicist's specific claim, which is about reasonable expectations, not the technology itself.
explanations.B: Reversed — this principle would support the platform's position, contradicting the ethicist's conclusion.
explanations.C: Reversed — the ethicist explicitly rejects the inference from legal permission to ethical permissibility; this principle would undermine the argument.
explanations.E: Tangential — the public/private domain distinction is not the basis of the ethicist's argument; the argument is about reasonable expectations at the time of consent, not the inherent nature of the domain.

difficultyReason: The argument involves a normative claim about scientific communication policy; distractors invoke plausible epistemic or institutional norms that don't license the specific conclusion.
stimulus: Science Journalist: A government health agency recently declined to publish a completed study on the long-term effects of a widely used food additive, citing concerns that the findings might cause public alarm before further research could confirm them. This decision was wrong. The public has been consuming the additive for decades and has a legitimate interest in knowing what researchers have found, even if the findings are preliminary.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the science journalist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Scientific findings that have not been replicated by independent researchers should not be released to the public under any circumstances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A public agency may withhold research findings only when releasing them would create a risk of harm that outweighs the public's interest in having the information.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government agencies have an absolute duty to publish all research they fund, regardless of the content or stage of the findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The potential to cause public alarm is never a legitimate reason for a government agency to withhold any type of information from the public.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preliminary scientific findings on matters that directly affect public health should not be suppressed by the agency responsible for that health domain solely to avoid causing concern.

explanations.correct: The journalist argues that the public's legitimate interest in research directly affecting their health overrides the agency's concern about premature alarm — particularly when the public has been exposed to the substance for decades. Principle E captures this precisely: health-relevant preliminary findings should not be suppressed by the responsible agency merely to prevent concern.
explanations.A: Reversed — this principle would support withholding findings that lack replication, directly contradicting the journalist's position.
explanations.B: This principle is compatible with the journalist's argument but does not license the conclusion as directly as E. It is a harm-balancing framework that could cut either way; E more precisely targets the journalist's specific claim about suppression to avoid concern.
explanations.C: Too broad — requiring publication of all funded research regardless of circumstances goes well beyond the journalist's argument, which is limited to research on public-health matters affecting current consumers.
explanations.D: Too broad — the journalist does not claim that preventing alarm is never a legitimate reason for any agency to withhold any information; the argument is specifically about a health agency withholding relevant health research.

difficultyReason: Argument involves a normative claim about institutional conflict of interest; distractors are closely related to ethics of funding but differ in scope or direction.
stimulus: Ethicist: A prominent nutrition research institute regularly publishes dietary guidelines that are adopted by public health agencies worldwide. The institute receives more than half of its annual funding from companies that manufacture processed food products. Even if the institute's researchers act in complete good faith, the institute should not be the body responsible for issuing these guidelines. The source of an institution's funding shapes the questions it asks and the conclusions it emphasizes, regardless of individual researchers' intentions.
questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Research institutions that accept private funding should disclose the identity of all donors in any publication resulting from that funding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An institution whose structural incentives are misaligned with the public interest should not hold authority over decisions that directly affect that public interest, even if its individual members act in good faith.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nutrition researchers who receive industry funding are more likely to produce biased results than researchers funded exclusively by government grants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public health agencies should evaluate the quality of dietary research solely on the basis of the methodological rigor of the studies they consider.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any institution that publishes guidelines adopted by government bodies must be subject to direct governmental oversight and regular independent audits.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's argument is that structural funding misalignment — not individual bad faith — disqualifies the institute from holding guideline authority. Principle B captures this structural logic: an institution with misaligned incentives should not hold public-interest authority regardless of its members' personal integrity.
explanations.A: Tangential — disclosure of donors is a transparency measure but does not address the disqualification claim the ethicist makes; the ethicist argues the institute should not hold authority, not merely that it should disclose funders.
explanations.C: Premise mismatch — the ethicist explicitly sets aside individual bad faith and bias; a principle about the likelihood of biased results is not what licenses the structural disqualification argument.
explanations.D: Reversed — this principle would support the institute's authority if its methodology is sound, which is precisely what the ethicist argues is insufficient.
explanations.E: Too narrow and tangential — governmental oversight and audits are procedural remedies that do not address whether the institution should hold authority in the first place.
